slots.title: Wages up 3.1% YoY; U-6 at 7.7%
slots.body:
August average hourly earnings, year over year: **3.1%** vs **3.0%** expected (prior **3.2%** in the calendar).

Month over month, wages rose **0.3%**, matching the **0.3%** estimate.

The U-6 unemployment rate—the measure that includes discouraged workers and part-timers who want full-time work—came in at **7.7%** vs **8.0%** expected (previous **7.9%**).

On the same day, Barron’s noted traders pricing roughly a three-in-five chance of a rate increase at the mid-September Fed meeting after the labor data.

Government payrolls added **35K** vs a **-11K** estimate.

Which wage or underemployment line do you pair with headline payrolls when the jobs report drops?

slots.title: U.S. cash session — Sept. 4, 2026
slots.body:
The U.S. cash session on **2026-09-04** centered on the **12:30** ET labor release.
Nonfarm payrolls printed **162K** jobs added in August versus a **56K** consensus; private payrolls **127K** vs **45K** expected.
Unemployment stayed at **4.1%**, matching the estimate.
Average hourly earnings rose **0.3%** month over month (estimate **0.3%**) and **3.1%** year over year (estimate **3.0%**).
U-6 unemployment was **7.7%** vs an **8.0%** estimate.

Major U.S. indexes closed lower after the data.
The S&P 500 finished at **7,717.81**, **-0.4%** (−**29.90** points), with an intraday span of **7,706.12** to **7,750.19**.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost **-0.5%** to **53,414.25** (−**271.86** points).
The Nasdaq Composite slipped **-0.3%** to **26,506.99**.
The Russell 2000 was an exception among U.S. benchmarks, **+0.2%** to **2,975.65**.

Sector averages on NASDAQ showed Utilities leading at roughly **+3.4%**, Financial Services about **+0.9%**, and Technology about **+0.7%**.
Lagging groups included Consumer Defensive near **-0.9%**, Consumer Cyclical near **-0.9%**, Energy near **-0.8%**, and Communication Services near **-0.6%**.
Healthcare was roughly flat (**0.0%**).

Megacap decliners included $TSLA **-5.9%** to **354.08**, $NFLX **-5.3%** to **78.25**, and $MSFT **-2.0%** to **499.70**.
$GOOG closed **-1.1%** at **335.31**.
Energy majors softened: $XOM **-1.7%** to **159.46**, $CVX **-1.3%** to **208.53**.

On the upside among large liquid names, $AMD **+4.7%** to **477.57**, $ASML **+4.2%** to **1,714.88**, and $ORCL **+3.1%** to **158.83**.
$META **+1.0%** to **616.77**; $NVDA **+0.8%** to **230.36**.
$AMZN was nearly unchanged at **258.51** (**-0.2%**).

Several non-megacap liquid losers stood out in the screen data, including $GWRE **-19.9%** to **162.42**, $LULU **-17.4%** to **100.61**, and $FICO **-16.7%** to **932.26**.
Active volume names in the feed included $NVDA, $INTC **+4.5%** to **95.80**, and leveraged $TSLA-linked products moving with the underlying.

Cross-asset, gold futures (GC) settled **-1.4%** at **4,476.60**.
Brent crude **+0.8%** to **96.28**; the USO ETF proxy for oil was **-0.1%** at **141.96**.
The dollar proxy UUP **+0.2%** to **28.08**.
Bitcoin **-0.1%** to **79,598.08**.

The CBOE VIX rose **+1.5%** to **14.53** (range **13.80**–**14.58**).
Treasury snapshot in the bundle (dated **2026-09-02**) showed the **10-year** at **4.8%** and the **2s10s spread** at **0.40** percentage points.

Overseas indexes in the same payload had already traded: Nikkei 225 **+1.3%** to **65,020.94**, Hang Seng **+1.7%** to **25,650.87**, FTSE 100 roughly flat at **10,831.09**.

News flow after the bell framed the U.S. equity decline alongside discussion of yields and September Fed meeting pricing following the jobs report; no additional earnings actuals were listed in the session earnings calendar field.

slots.title: August CPI Report Still on Deck
slots.body:
The **August CPI report** is still the next big inflation print in focus — it tracks how much everyday prices rose over the month.

Coverage cites an expectation for **headline CPI around 3.6%**, with energy costs called out as a driver in that write-up.

The same piece also points to **super-core PCE inflation at 3.9%** as a gauge of stickier, wage-linked price pressure.

Friday’s jobs data already showed **+3.1%** year-over-year average hourly earnings — a separate labor-cost line markets often read next to CPI.

When the August CPI number posts, it resolves the month’s official consumer-inflation story alongside that wage print.

Which inflation line do you watch first — headline CPI or the wage side from payrolls?
